title: Repeated, high-grade recycling of mixed steel scrap

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a practical system that repeatedly turns heterogeneous steel scrap into steel suitable for demanding applications. It would remove or manage persistent contaminants, especially copper, while retaining a high proportion of the metal and meeting the composition and performance requirements of the intended product. Its defining capability is to maintain quality across successive recycling cycles despite variation in incoming scrap.

The system could span scrap preparation, refining and product qualification. Copper removal would be one component of the broader capability: success with a single contaminant would not establish control of multiple impurities or consistent production from mixed feeds. The supplied 2024 report provides a concrete motivation, describing copper accumulation in recycled steel and an electrochemical approach intended to expand access to higher-grade products.

significance.text: If mixed, contaminated scrap could reliably become demanding steel grades again, secondary steel feedstock would become more flexible and useful. The supplied report connects copper removal with potential automotive and transport applications. Achieving the broader capability could let steel circulate through such uses repeatedly, reducing the extent to which scrap composition restricts the next product that can be made.

As a conditional consequence of the proposed capability, effective impurity control could reduce dependence on virgin iron added to dilute contaminants. It could also widen the range of scrap streams that producers can accept. Whether those changes deliver competitive costs or lower life-cycle emissions would depend on the complete process, including preparation, refining, energy consumption, metal losses and residue treatment; those benefits are requirements to demonstrate, rather than established outcomes.

The material-balance limit remains important: better recycling does not create additional iron. Primary iron could still be needed when steel demand grows faster than recoverable scrap supply, or when collection and recovery leave insufficient usable material. The revolutionary advance would therefore be sustained access to high-grade uses from secondary feedstock, without implying the elimination of primary iron production or an indefinitely lossless material loop.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target is economical impurity control at large scale across heterogeneous feeds and repeated cycles. The supplied report identifies copper accumulation as a barrier and states that traditional electric arc furnace steelmaking cannot remove copper from molten scrap. The research notes explain this in terms of the difficulty of removing copper through ordinary oxidation-based refining, but the supplied review does not directly substantiate that mechanism. The documented limitation of traditional practice is sufficient to motivate the concept without treating the mechanistic explanation as independently verified here.

Engineering synthesis: a convincing solution must control several contaminants while coping with changing scrap compositions, preserve useful metal recovery and produce material that passes the requirements of the selected grades. Removing an impurity from the metal also requires accounting for where it goes and how the resulting streams are handled. The practical challenge is to combine these functions at useful throughput and acceptable total cost, rather than optimizing a single removal step in isolation.

For the reported electrochemical route, questions requiring demonstration include sustained operation, electrolyte and cell durability, energy demand, separation efficiency and integration into a steelmaking process. These are proposed engineering evaluation areas, not failures established by the supplied evidence. Extending removal to additional contaminants is a distinct scientific task: the 2024 report presents tin removal as future work, so its copper-focused account cannot establish comprehensive impurity control.

current_state.text: A University of Toronto Engineering report reproduced by SciTechDaily on June 22, 2024 identifies Jaesuk Paeng, William D. Judge and Gisele Azimi's paper, “Electrorefining for copper tramp element removal from molten iron for green steelmaking,” DOI: 10.1016/j.resconrec.2024.107654. According to the supplied review, the report describes an oxysulfide-electrolyte approach to removing copper and carbon from molten iron. This is a dated research approach toward one part of the broader recycling capability.

The report describes a cell designed to bring copper below 0.1 wt%. That number should be read as the reported design objective; the supplied review does not provide primary experimental results sufficient to establish its achievement, repeatability, throughput or applicability across mixed scrap compositions. The report also describes removal of other contaminants, including tin, as future work. It does not demonstrate a mixed-feed, multi-impurity industrial system operating through repeated recycling cycles.

The supplied review had a complete retained copy of the institutional news report, with no recorded extraction issues or truncation. The primary paper's methods and results were not available within the supplied review evidence. Earlier notes say that a publisher page could not be opened and that an accessible abstract had been used, but that access history and abstract inspection could not be independently checked in the review. Consequently, the news report supports the identity and reported direction of the work, while leaving its detailed experimental performance unassessed.

Evidence limitation: no subsequent-development or bounded freshness search results were supplied. The material therefore does not establish whether the complete capability remained unavailable as of November 1, 2026, nor does it establish later commercial readiness. This absence of an update leaves present availability unresolved; it is not evidence that the reported research result is false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a commercial-scale system on representative mixed steel scrap and produce multiple demanding steel grades that meet predefined composition and product-performance requirements. Feed selection should cover a declared range of contaminant mixtures and concentrations, with enough variation to test the claimed operating envelope. These are proposed criteria for this innovation, not established industry standards or thresholds endorsed by the supplied source.
completion_criteria.label: Commercial-scale mixed-scrap processing produces multiple qualified demanding steel grades

completion_criteria.text: Proposed repeated-cycle test: recycle the resulting steel through successive, traceable cycles and account for impurity concentrations and metal flows at each stage. Within the declared operating envelope, the system should avoid systematic impurity accumulation without relying on virgin-metal dilution to meet the selected specifications. Any such additions should be disclosed so that their contribution can be distinguished from actual contaminant removal or management. A finite campaign would establish the demonstrated range of feeds, grades and cycles, rather than literal universality or unlimited recyclability.
completion_criteria.label: Successive traceable recycling cycles avoid impurity accumulation without virgin-metal dilution

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical validation: independent accounting should establish metal recovery, throughput, energy and consumable requirements, residue quantities and handling, total costs and life-cycle emissions. The meanings of high recovery, competitive cost and low emissions should be defined before testing against relevant production alternatives and consistent accounting boundaries. Reproducibility should include independently checked measurements and repeat campaigns, with the limits of feed tolerance, product qualification and sustained operation stated explicitly.
completion_criteria.label: Independent practical validation reports full resource costs and operating limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: MET-10, “Repeated upcycling of mixed aluminum scrap into demanding alloys,” is the closest conceptual parallel because both seek repeated recovery of demanding alloy uses from mixed scrap. They remain separate innovations involving different base metals and metallurgical systems. Only MET-10's title is supplied, so no specific aluminum refining mechanism, maturity or performance comparison can be established.

Roster-based comparison: MET-02, “Steel from ore without fossil carbon at competitive global scale,” concerns primary steel production, whereas MET-03 concerns recovering quality from existing steel. The two could complement one another where recoverable scrap cannot meet demand. MET-01, “Predictive metallurgy from composition to lifetime,” concerns predicting material behavior; such predictions could assist qualification of recycled steel, but would not themselves demonstrate impurity removal or repeated recycling.

Roster-based comparison: MET-04, “Structural metals that repeatedly heal fatigue damage in service,” MET-06, “A practical structural alloy system for sustained fusion-reactor conditions,” MET-09, “Uncoated structural alloys for very high temperatures in oxidizing environments,” and MET-11, “Structural alloys with broadly reliable intrinsic corrosion resistance,” focus on material behavior during service. MET-03 focuses on recovering feedstock quality between uses. Recycling performance would not establish self-healing, fusion suitability, high-temperature oxidation resistance or intrinsic corrosion resistance; those require separate demonstrations.

Roster-based comparison: MET-05, “Titanium at mass-market structural-metal cost,” targets the economics of another structural metal. MET-07, “Manufacturable, damage-tolerant bulk metallic glasses,” targets a material class and its manufacturability and damage tolerance. MET-08, “Practical room-temperature superplastic forming of common alloys,” targets forming behavior. Their broad overlap with MET-03 is the pursuit of more useful or economical structural materials, while their defining advances remain distinct from repeated impurity control in steel scrap. These comparisons are limited to the supplied roster titles.

unresolved_issues: The primary paper's experimental copper concentrations, removal efficiency, metal recovery, energy demand, throughput and repeatability cannot be established from the supplied review.
Whether copper below 0.1 wt% was experimentally achieved, and under what feed and operating conditions, remains unresolved here.
The broader economic, yield and multi-impurity constraints are appropriate evaluation targets but are not quantitatively characterized by the supplied evidence.
No supplied freshness record establishes subsequent progress, commercial availability or continued absence of the complete capability through November 1, 2026.
The earlier publisher-access failure and abstract inspection remain reported access history rather than independently verified review findings.
Representative feed ranges, selected steel grades, cycle counts, commercial throughput and quantitative cost, recovery and emissions criteria must be defined before a completion campaign.
Detailed relationships to MET-10 and the other roster concepts remain unassessed beyond their supplied titles.

brief.title: Recycling mixed steel scrap into high-quality steel again
possible: Steel from mixed scrap could return to demanding uses, such as car bodies and transport equipment, through repeated rounds of recycling. Producers could keep meeting each product’s composition and performance requirements as the scrap supply changes.
why: Copper builds up as steel is recycled and can damage its properties. Controlling it and other impurities would give steelmakers more freedom to use mixed scrap and keep that steel circulating through high-quality products.
Effective impurity removal could also reduce the need to add newly produced iron to dilute contamination, while widening the range of scrap that producers can accept.

sources.who: Jaesuk Paeng, William D. Judge and Gisele Azimi
sources.showed: The University of Toronto team reported using electricity and a slag-based material to remove copper from molten iron. Slag is a steelmaking waste.
sources.quote: “Our study is the first reported instance of electrochemically removing copper from steel and reducing impurities to below alloy level,”
sources.cited_for: The work supports an electrical route for removing copper that restricts recycled steel’s uses.
sources.not_established: The work does not establish reliable production from mixed scrap across repeated recycling cycles.

sources.who: Tohoku University and Infineon Technologies Japan researchers
sources.showed: Immersion in molten lead removed the copper layer from copper-coated steel samples. The researchers observed negligible iron loss into the bath and little lead entering the steel.
sources.quote:
In the Cu-clad steel sample, the Cu layer was completely 
removed by immersion
sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates copper removal from steel with a firmly bonded copper layer.
sources.not_established: The sample tests do not establish large-scale treatment of varied scrap or quality across repeated recycling cycles.

sources.who: Hongyan Sun, Xiaojun Hu and Zhongzi Chen
sources.showed: The University of Science and Technology Beijing team removed some copper from molten steel using a chemical mixture that converts copper into compounds that leave as vapour.
sources.quote: Experimental results demonstrated an ideal copper removal ratio of 39.68% under optimized conditions
sources.cited_for: The experiments support chemical removal of copper already dissolved in liquid steel.
sources.not_established: Partial copper removal does not establish control of several impurities or prevention of buildup through repeated recycling.

sources.showed: The Iwate University team measured how copper, tin and zinc divide between molten iron and lead. Copper and tin concentrated in the lead.
sources.quote:
Tin content in the molten iron can be
reduced to about one-third by this solvent extraction.
sources.cited_for: The work supports transferring several impurities from molten iron into lead.
sources.not_established: Lead remaining in the iron still required removal, and repeated production of qualified steel was not demonstrated.

shown: Researchers have demonstrated separate ways to tackle copper. Toronto’s team reported electrical removal from molten iron. Tohoku-led researchers removed a bonded copper layer in sample tests, while the Beijing team removed part of the copper dissolved in liquid steel.

Iwate researchers also measured the transfer of several impurities into molten lead. These results establish individual separation steps. Their performance as a complete, repeatedly operating recycling system remains to be demonstrated.
missing: Commercial-scale production must turn varied mixed scrap into several steel grades that pass composition and performance tests.
Traceable recycling cycles must maintain quality without impurity buildup or dilution with newly produced iron.
Independent trials must establish metal recovery, sustained output, resource use, residue handling, costs and emissions.

milestones.label: Mixed scrap produces several qualified steel grades at commercial scale
milestones.explanation: A commercial-scale system would have to make several demanding steel grades from scrap with varied contamination. Passing composition and performance tests would establish its useful operating range.

milestones.label: Repeated recycling avoids impurity buildup without newly produced iron
milestones.explanation: Successive, traceable cycles would have to track metal and impurities while meeting specifications without dilution by newly produced iron. This would establish that quality survives repeated recycling.

milestones.label: Independent trials establish full costs and operating limits
milestones.explanation: Independent repeat trials would have to account for metal recovery, output, energy, consumables, residues, costs and life-cycle emissions. Comparison against predefined criteria would establish practical performance and limits.

uncertain: Can impurity removal remain effective as scrap composition changes and several contaminants occur together?
Can the processes sustain useful output while retaining enough metal and keeping total costs and emissions acceptable?
Which scrap mixtures, steel grades and cycle counts would adequately demonstrate lasting quality?

page.title: Repeated recycling of mixed steel scrap into flat steel
page.definition: A system repeatedly converts mixed post-consumer steel scrap into flat steel—sheet or strip—that meets a specified grade’s chemical, mechanical and surface-quality requirements. It controls tramp elements, unwanted residual metals such as copper and tin, without virgin-iron dilution.

goal.need: A 2019 assessment reports a greater than fourfold gap between typical shredded scrap’s copper content and the limits for many flat-steel products. Its dilution example requires 3 tonnes of primary steel per tonne of contaminated steel to reach 0.1 wt% copper. Separating contaminants could reduce this primary-metal requirement while allowing post-consumer scrap to supply flat-steel products.

figures.caption: Representative copper concentrations reported in the 2019 assessment.
figures.note: wt% means mass percent. Product limits depend on the steel grade.

statements.quote: Develop industrial and economic feasible solutions for refining steel melts to remove non-volatile tramp elements like copper and tin;
targeting high quality of the finished product and reduced CO2 emissions.
statements.context: The work programme seeks increased utilisation of low-quality scrap through new technologies and steelmaking routes.

completion.title: Mixed scrap returns to the same qualified flat-steel grade through successive recycling cycles.
completion.criterion: An operating plant processes a declared range of mixed post-consumer steel scrap through traceable successive recycling cycles into the same specified flat-steel grade. Each pass meets that grade’s published chemical, mechanical and surface-quality requirements without adding virgin iron to dilute tramp elements. Iron and contaminant balances include fresh scrap inputs, returned steel, rejected fractions and residues, distinguishing removal and separation from dilution. The claim covers only the demonstrated feeds and cycles.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; proposed operational repeat-cycle test because no external acceptance criterion for the complete capability was found.
completion.basis: Searched ESTEP roadmaps, Clean Steel Partnership calls, PURESCRAP and MEDALS targets, and public ISO/ASTM scrap and recycling standard scopes for a repeat-cycle acceptance test. None specified a complete test or required cycle count for this capability. The proposed test covers one specified flat-steel grade over documented successive cycles, excluding virgin-iron dilution; it claims no universal yield, cost or throughput threshold.

milestones.title: A steel-scrap impurity-control operation has experimental proof of concept.
milestones.criterion: An impurity-control operation has experimental proof of concept (TRL 3). Yamaguchi and Takeda (2003) used about 6 g Fe–C alloy and 6 g Pb at 1453 K and reported Pb/Fe distribution ratios of 2.16 for Cu and 2.24 for Sn. Sun et al. (2025) treated 150 g steel at 1873 K and removed up to 44.57% Cu in 30 min. Ushikubo et al. (2026) removed a Cu-clad specimen’s copper layer in a 100 g Pb bath at 1273 K for 10 min. These results establish individual laboratory operations.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, Horizon Europe General Annex B, Technology Readiness Levels; the generic proof-of-concept criterion is applied here to scrap impurity control, without claiming an official TRL assessment of these studies.

milestones.title: Classified scrap meets PURESCRAP’s copper, molybdenum, nickel and tin limits.
milestones.criterion: Produce classified scrap containing Cu ≤0.05 wt%, Mo <0.02 wt%, Ni <0.1 wt% and Sn <0.03 wt%. These are PURESCRAP’s scrap-product targets, rather than universal finished-steel specifications. On 1 September 2026, the consortium reported that final sorting and melting trial timelines were being coordinated; that project news item, which is not peer reviewed, supplies no result establishing simultaneous achievement of the four limits.
milestones.set_by: Horizon Europe PURESCRAP consortium, Deliverable 1.4, Table 1, page 11; targets for its scrap-classification route, published only in a table.

milestones.title: Steelmaking at TRL 6 raises low-quality scrap’s input share by at least 25% against usual practice.
milestones.criterion: For a specified steel quality, increase low-quality post-consumer scrap’s share of total scrap input by at least 25% compared with usual practice, at technology readiness level 6. TRL 6 requires demonstration in an industrially relevant environment. The roadmap does not specify whether the increase denotes a relative percentage or percentage points.
milestones.set_by: European Commission–ESTEP Clean Steel Partnership, targets reproduced in ESTEP’s June 2021 EAF scrap-route roadmap, Table 1, page 21; numerical threshold published only in a table. TRL meaning follows Horizon Europe General Annex B.

milestones.title: A qualified TRL 8 system raises low-quality scrap’s input share by at least 50% against usual practice.
milestones.criterion: At TRL 8, the system is complete and qualified, and low-quality scrap’s share of total scrap input increases by at least 50% against usual practice for a specified steel quality. BMW reported on 10 August 2026 that its Car2Car campaign covered 433 vehicles from 60 models, including test vehicles; recovered steel passed material and quality testing and supplied more than 100,000 series parts. This developer press release is not peer reviewed and establishes neither the roadmap’s 50% comparison nor successive recycling cycles.
milestones.set_by: European Commission–ESTEP Clean Steel Partnership, targets reproduced in ESTEP’s June 2021 EAF scrap-route roadmap, Table 1, page 21; numerical threshold published only in a table. TRL meaning follows Horizon Europe General Annex B.

not_found: Publisher access to the 2024 Toronto electrorefining paper was blocked; its primary experimental performance could not be checked.
The Car2Car final-report links opened without readable text; the industrial result therefore rests on BMW’s press release.
No opened result verifies all four PURESCRAP chemistry limits or either ESTEP scrap-share comparison.
The full requirements of ISO 59014 and ASTM E702 were not opened; the standards search covered their public scopes.

results.finding: Electrorefining removed copper from iron to below 0.1 wt%; sample size not reported.
results.detail: The source reports a laboratory impurity-control operation and attributes the result to a published journal study. It does not state the sample size.
results.quote: To remove copper from iron to below 0.1 wt%, the team had to first design an electrochemical cell that could withstand temperatures up to 1600 degrees Celsius.

results.finding: One Cu-clad steel sample: the copper layer was completely removed in a 100 g molten Pb bath.
results.detail: Immersion was at 1273 K for 10 minutes under argon. SEM-EDS indicated negligible Fe dissolution and little Pb diffusion into the steel.
results.quote:
In the Cu-clad steel sample, the Cu layer was completely 
removed by immersion at 1273 K for 10 min.

results.finding: Selective chlorination removed up to 44.57% of copper from a 150 g liquid-steel sample.
results.detail: The laboratory experiment used prepared copper-containing steel at 1873 K for 30 minutes.
results.quote:
After continuous oxidation and chlorination for 30 min, the maximum copper removal ratio of 44.57% was achieved at n(Fe
2
O
3
)/n(Cu) of 10.0.

results.finding: Lead-solvent extraction using about 6 g each of Fe–C alloy and lead produced a Cu distribution ratio of 2.16.
results.detail: The experiment was conducted at 1453 K. The measured Sn distribution ratio was 2.24; removing residual lead from the iron remained future work.
results.quote:
Distribution ratios of copper, tin and zinc between
the lead and the iron phases are 2.16, 2.24 and 1.42,
respectively.

results.finding: Vacuum distillation of 10–60 kg melted steel scrap removed 70–90% of initial copper.
results.detail: Experiments used melt temperatures of 1850–2050 K and chamber pressures of 3–400 Pa, with 30 minutes of vacuum exposure.
results.quote: The experiments found that 70 to 90 pct of initial copper, 60 to 80 pct of initial tin, 80 to 100 pct of initial managanese, and 20 to 40 pct of initial sulfur can be eliminated in 30 minutes exposure to vacuum.

results.finding: Vacuum distillation of 10–60 kg melted scrap samples removed 70–90% of initial copper; the number of melts was not stated.
results.detail: The experiments also removed tin, but report no final concentrations or molybdenum and nickel results. They do not establish a classified scrap product meeting all four limits.
results.quote: The experiments found that 70 to 90 pct of initial copper, 60 to 80 pct of initial tin, 80 to 100 pct of initial managanese, and 20 to 40 pct of initial sulfur can be eliminated in 30 minutes exposure to vacuum.
